title: Scout recent JDM research gaps (@general subagent)

data.text:
You are scouting for a NOVEL, publishable judgment-and-decision-making (JDM) research question that can be answered WITHOUT collecting new data (secondary analysis of openly licensed data, or a simulation/agent-based model). Context: three prior papers already exist in sibling folders and must NOT be duplicated (read their novelty.md files to confirm): (1) ~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper (anchoring-proportionality meta-analysis of OpAQ); (2) ~/Documents/Coding/[other project] (GJP forecasting, belief-movement by horizon); (3) ~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper3 (selective feedback / comparative advisor evaluation simulation). Do NOT propose topics in anchoring, probability forecasting/GJP, or advisor-verification/selective-feedback.

TASK: Identify 5-8 candidate research questions that are (a) genuinely understudied, (b) answerable with an openly licensed dataset OR a falsifiable simulation, (c) in the JDM space (judgment: heuristics, biases, confidence, calibration, advice, aggregation, information search; decision-making: risk, intertemporal choice, framing, strategic/social decisions, metacognition). For each candidate give: the question, why it is novel (name the closest paper and its gap), what data/model it needs, and whether it could fail/be refuted.

METHOD: Use the OpenAlex API (no key needed for basic queries, or load keys via `set -a; source ~/.claude/api_keys.env; set +a`). Query recent works (2023-2026) in JDM outlets. Useful approach: fetch recent issues/works for journals "Judgment and Decision Making", "Journal of Behavioral Decision Making", "Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes", "Cognitive Psychology", "Cognition", "Psychological Science", "Management Science". Use webfetch on OpenAlex URLs like https://api.openalex.org/works?filter=primary_location.source.id:...&per-page=50 . Also run targeted searches for candidate topics. Verify any DOI you mention resolves (https://api.crossref.org/works/{DOI}).

OUTPUT: Write your full report to ~/Documents/Coding/ai-jdm-paper4/scoping/literature_scout.md and return a concise summary (the 5-8 candidates with one-line novelty + data). Be honest about what is already done; do not overclaim novelty. Cite DOIs.

# Novelty: the five closest papers and what this study adds

Search basis (2026-09-27; Imhoff & Barker, 2023, added on 2026-09-28 after the published version of one source study was found): OpenAlex, Google Scholar and Semantic Scholar citers of the OpAQ data paper (24 works) and of the OpAQ meta-analysis preprint; OpenAlex citers since 2022 of Lieder et al. (2018a; 164), Lieder et al. (2018b; 21) and Turner & Schley (2016; 54); keyword and web searches for computational models of anchoring and for anchor extremity. Full reports are in `scoping/`. DOIs were checked against Crossref. No work was found that relates the proportional anchoring index to anchor extremity across many items with trial-level data, or that compares process models on OpAQ.

| # | Paper | What it did | What this study adds |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Röseler, L., & Schütz, A. (2022). Hanging the anchor off a new ship: A meta-analysis of anchoring effects. PsyArXiv. https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/wf2tn | Meta-analysis of the OpAQ data (90 studies, k = 386 items, N = 17,708). Hedges' g rose with the mean relative distance between anchor and true value (b = 0.040 per unit, k = 312). Concluded against the prediction that extreme anchors give smaller effects, and called for a unitless "relative strength of adjustment" metric to formalise how adjustment depends on anchor distance. | g is a standardised mean difference, so it rises with anchor distance even when anchors pull estimates by a constant proportion. We measure the proportional pull directly (log-scale elasticity and anchoring index), separate within-item from across-item variation, and test the pattern against pre-computed predictions of five process models. |
| 2 | Schley, D. R., & Weingarten, E. (2026). Fifty years of anchoring effects: A theoretical reintegration and meta-analysis. Management Science (online 2026-05-19). https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.03238 | Meta-analysis of 1,280 high-vs-low effect sizes (482 studies). Extremity was a binary flag (49 of 1,280 effect sizes "extreme"); coefficient -0.02 [-0.20, 0.16]. An earlier version added a meta-study with 8 items and anchors at calibration percentiles; the high-minus-low gap in z-scored estimates grew with extremity. Theories were compared qualitatively; the authors call for formal models. | Continuous, outcome-free extremity (log distance of anchor from truth) instead of a binary author label; a proportional outcome instead of g or z-scores; trial-level data from many studies; formal models whose predictions are simulated on the actual designs and frozen before the data are read. |
| 3 | Barrera-Lemarchand, F., Balenzuela, P., Bahrami, B., Deroy, O., & Navajas, J. (2024). Promoting erroneous divergent opinions increases the wisdom of crowds. Psychological Science, 35, 872-886. https://doi.org/10.1177/09567976241252138 | Modelled the anchored crowd mean as a weighted average of anchor and crowd mean with weight w0·exp(-beta·|A - truth|). In 30 percentage questions with anchors fixed at 5% and 95% (N = 396), the anchoring weight fell with anchor distance (r = -.56). | Their distance varied only through the true value on a bounded 0-100 scale, which can compress responses mechanically. We use open-ended ratio-scale quantities, vary the anchor itself within items (up to 20 anchor levels, and continuous random anchors), and compare this discounting pattern with rival models that predict rising or constant proportional influence. |
| 4 | Lieder, F., Griffiths, T. L., Huys, Q. J. M., & Goodman, N. D. (2018). The anchoring bias reflects rational use of cognitive resources. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 25, 322-349. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-017-1286-8 | Resource-rational anchoring-and-adjustment: a sampling chain starts at the anchor and stops after the number of adjustments that balances error and time cost. Fitted Jacowitz & Kahneman's (1995) anchoring index for 15 quantities (predicted 53.2% vs observed 48.5%). Stated that bias grows in proportion to anchor distance for a fixed number of adjustments; did not derive or test how the proportional index changes with extremity. | We derive the extremity prediction for two variants: a fixed number of adjustments (proportional pull rises with extremity) and an adaptive, resource-rational number (proportional pull falls). We test both on data with many anchor levels per item. |
| 5 | Imhoff, R., & Barker, P. (2023). Connecting the dots: Nonlinear patterns in the presence of symbolic and nonsymbolic numerical standards. Judgment and Decision Making, 18, e34. https://doi.org/10.1017/jdm.2023.31 | Study 2 (N = 803): participants estimated dot patterns of about 500 dots next to standards that differed by up to 400 dots in 20-dot steps, each labelled with its exact number (a symbolic anchor). Estimates assimilated to the anchor, with a cubic pattern that levelled off beyond a difference of about 300 dots. This is the closest precedent for a within-item extremity function with many anchor levels. | Their evidence covers one perceptual quantity (dot numerosity) with anchors between about 0.2 and 1.8 times the target, on a z-scored raw scale. We test the shape for general-knowledge magnitudes with anchors up to several orders of magnitude from the truth, with a proportional outcome, pooled over 20 item-study cells, and against pre-computed predictions of five process models. The OpAQ cell labelled "Imhoff & Barker, Study 2" is a separate general-knowledge item (height of Cologne cathedral, 20 anchor levels) from a side task in the same study. |

Röseler et al. (2025, Meta-Psychology, https://doi.org/10.15626/MP.2024.4137) formalised and falsified a time-based insufficient-adjustment model without addressing extremity. Wu et al. (2026, Cognitive Science, https://doi.org/10.1111/cogs.70229) found anchoring scores rising linearly with anchor offset for one perceptual quantity (virtual-reality height estimation).

# Novelty: the five closest papers and what this study adds

Study: a preregistered secondary analysis of the Good Judgment Project (GJP) forecast data. It tests whether individual forecasters revise their probabilities too much when a question's resolution is far away and too little when it is near. Augenblick, Lazarus and Thaler (2025) predict this pattern from over-inference from weak signals and under-inference from strong signals. It is tested with the excess-movement statistic of Augenblick and Rabin (2021), with the window regression of Augenblick et al. (2025), and with calibration slopes by horizon. A simulation on the actual GJP report schedule, frozen before the forecasts were read, shows which forecaster models produce which pattern.

Search record: `scoping/literature_gaps.md` (section 1) and `scoping/crowding_gjp.md` (citing-paper screens of both key papers in OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, OpenCitations and RePEc; web searches across forecasting platforms and datasets; 28 September 2026). No located work computes excess movement by horizon for individual forecasters. All DOIs below were resolved on Crossref.

| # | Paper | What it did | What this study adds |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Augenblick, N., & Rabin, M. (2021). Belief movement, uncertainty reduction, and rational updating. *Quarterly Journal of Economics*, 136(2), 933–985. https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjaa043 | Derived the excess-movement test of Bayesian updating and applied it to pooled GJP forecasts (593,218 assessments, 3,408 forecasters, 291 events): movement exceeded uncertainty reduction by 20%. | Splits excess movement by the time left until the question's scheduled close, restricted to forecasters who worked alone, so the result speaks to how updating changes with signal strength rather than to its average. Adds the training contrast and a reconstruction of their pooled statistic as a check. |
| 2 | Augenblick, N., Lazarus, E., & Thaler, M. (2025). Overinference from weak signals and underinference from strong signals. *Quarterly Journal of Economics*, 140(1), 335–401. https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjae032 | Showed over-inference from weak and under-inference from strong signals in experiments, and in Betfair and option prices, using time to resolution as the proxy for signal strength. Noted that the market results are "at minimum directionally informative" about individual beliefs. | Tests the prediction on individual, non-market probability reports in the field, with their own window regression. Separates the pattern from time-decay neglect (fixed-date versus deadline questions) and from a static compression of reports (calibration by horizon), using simulated predictions of each account on the same design. |
| 3 | Atanasov, P., Witkowski, J., Ungar, L., Mellers, B., & Tetlock, P. (2020). Small steps to accuracy: Incremental belief updaters are better forecasters. *Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes*, 160, 19–35. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.obhdp.2020.02.001 | In GJP, forecasters who updated often and in small steps were more accurate; training reduced update size by about 12%. | Judges updates against the Bayesian benchmark (movement relative to uncertainty reduction) instead of by size, and asks how this changes with horizon and whether training moves forecasters towards the benchmark or past it. |
| 4 | Moore, D. A., Swift, S. A., Minster, A., Mellers, B., Ungar, L., Tetlock, P., Yang, H. H. J., & Tenney, E. R. (2017). Confidence calibration in a multiyear geopolitical forecasting competition. *Management Science*, 63(11), 3552–3565. https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2016.2525 | Described GJP calibration over the life of a question: extreme forecasts made early were especially inaccurate, and confidence and accuracy rose together over time. | Links calibration by horizon to belief movement. The signal-strength account predicts overconfidence far from resolution and underconfidence near it; a static compression of reports predicts underconfidence throughout. This study tests both against frozen predictions. |
| 5 | Atanasov, P., & Himmelstein, M. (2023). Talent spotting in crowd prediction. In M. Seifert (Ed.), *Judgment in predictive analytics* (pp. 135–184). Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-30085-1_6 | Used the Augenblick–Rabin statistic per GJP forecaster as a stable skill marker (reliability .85; correlation with accuracy .30–.40). | Treats excess movement as a within-forecaster process that depends on horizon rather than as a trait, and estimates it separately for each horizon band. |

Other close work, cited in the manuscript where relevant: Satopää et al. (2021, BIN model, accuracy components by horizon in GJP; https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2020.3882); Halperin and Mazlish (2025 working paper; the same sign pattern by horizon in consensus macroeconomic forecasts); Casey (2021; professional forecasters overconfident at long and underconfident at short horizons, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijforecast.2020.09.002).

Limits of the novelty claim: groups that hold the GJP data (Augenblick and co-authors; the Tetlock and Mellers group) may have unpublished analyses of this question; the citation indices searched cover fewer papers than Google Scholar, which could not be queried.

# Novelty assessment before preregistration

Search completed 28 September 2026; primary sources, queries, metadata, and caveats are preserved in `scoping/literature_agent.md` and `scoping/journal_and_data.md`. This is a scoped search, not proof that no prior paper contains the same result. No hypothesis-bearing simulation or participant-level outcome was examined.

## Study contribution

The paper distinguishes two targets of learning from selectively verified advice: absolute advisor accuracy and the sign of the advisor's accuracy advantage over oneself. It derives the limits of paired comparison and quantifies finite-feedback decision loss when correction for confidence selection trades reduced bias for additional variance. A future randomised feedback-display experiment supplies refutable psychological predictions. The mathematical identity, inverse-probability weighting, and the general fact that selection biases learning are existing ideas, not claimed inventions.

## Five closest papers

1. **Pescetelli & Yeung (2021), The role of decision confidence in advice-taking and trust formation.** DOI: https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0000960. Their experiments and models concern confidence-weighted agreement as evidence of advisor reliability, including learning without objective feedback and distortion from dependent judgements. **Addition:** objective truth is available but selectively sampled; compare absolute and paired representations of the same verified cases and state their different estimands. This is not the first computational model of confidence and trust.

2. **Jaquiery & Yeung (2024), Preferences for advisor agreement and accuracy.** DOI: https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0311211. Their experiments distinguish agreement and accuracy with and without feedback; feedback supports preference for accuracy. **Addition:** distinguish feedback's presence from its selection mechanism; uniform disagreement feedback can remain adequate for relative ranking even when inappropriate for absolute assessment. No claim that their participants exhibited the proposed selection effect.

3. **Fetchenhauer & Dunning (2010), Why so cynical? Asymmetric feedback underlies misguided skepticism regarding the trustworthiness of others.** DOI: https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797609358586. Their trust experiments show that feedback conditional on trusting can sustain inaccurate negative impressions. **Addition:** advisor verification offers a paired contrast whose unobserved values on agreement are structurally zero, so missing feedback need not undermine the comparative decision. Reciprocity and classification accuracy are distinct tasks; this paper does not reproduce their experiment.

4. **Gao et al. (2021), Human-AI Collaboration with Bandit Feedback.** DOI: https://doi.org/10.24963/ijcai.2021/237. They use counterfactual policy learning to route cases between humans and machines under bandit feedback. **Addition:** a constrained global advisor-adoption decision, with fully verified paired labels on sampled cases, psychologically interpretable absolute/paired summaries, and finite-label cost of selection adjustment. IPW itself and learning from selectively observed outcomes are established; no general policy-learning advance is claimed.

5. **Zavattari, Tommasi, & Prencipe (2026), One Human, N Agents: Audit-Budget Allocation for LLM Agent Fleets under Miscalibrated, Correlated Confidence.** Primary preprint: https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28317. It already models budgeted inspections, confidence selection, correlated errors, and worse-than-random auditing. **Addition:** learning comparative competence from a feedback history rather than allocating inspections to reduce remaining errors across a fleet; paired representation and the zero contribution of agreements are central. This is an unreviewed preprint, and its DOI belongs to DataCite rather than Crossref; registry coverage must not be misrepresented.

## Further overlap and limits

Denrell & March (2001) and Denrell (2005) already explain biased impressions through selective experience. Fok & Weld (2024) discuss verification and complementary performance. Honeycutt et al. (2020) show that interactive feedback can reduce trust and perceived accuracy. Li & Steyvers (2026, preprint) model learning AI confidence calibration. These precedents restrict the contribution to a particular representation-by-selection boundary and its finite-feedback consequences.

A transparent two-stratum scenario is intentionally limited. The paper cannot establish which summaries humans use, how often real verification follows the assumed policies, or that its numerical worlds describe deployed AI. It should be judged as a computational Theory Article with a testable behavioural extension, not as empirical evidence of algorithm aversion.

## Post-preregistration literature addendum: selective-feedback coding

Added during the first manuscript review, after preregistration and confirmatory analysis, on 28 September 2026. This supplements the original five-paper assessment without changing the preregistration or the simulations.

**Elwin, Juslin, Olsson, and Enkvist (2007), Constructivist coding: Learning from selective feedback**, [10.1111/j.1467-9280.2007.01856.x](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9280.2007.01856.x), is a substantive predecessor. Their investment task contrasted complete with decision-contingent feedback. Performance was not demonstrably impaired by selective feedback, and behaviour was better captured by reconstructing missing outcomes from task knowledge than by merely recording observed outcomes. Their design also approximately matched feedback counts by allowing more training opportunities under selection. Primary full text and Crossref metadata were checked; see `manuscript/reference_audit.md`.

**Implication for contribution:** The general claims that selective experience need not damage decisions, that feedback representation matters, and that label-matched comparisons are useful are already established. This paper's narrower addition concerns absolute advisor accuracy versus the sign of a paired advisor–self accuracy difference, including the zero contribution of agreement cases and the finite-sample consequences of confidence-dependent selection within disagreements. Elwin et al. reconstruct unobserved outcomes for task learning and base-rate inference; the paired source-comparison identity and present estimator comparison are different. Their evidence is also a reason to treat the absolute learner as an experimental benchmark rather than an established default account of human learning.

Search record: `scoping/literature_gaps.md` (section 1) and `scoping/crowding_gjp.md` (citing-paper screens of both key papers in OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, OpenCitations and RePEc; web searches across forecasting platforms and datasets; 28 September 2026). No located work computes excess movement by horizon for individual forecasters. All DOIs below were resolved on Crossref.

| # | Paper | What it did | What this study adds |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Augenblick, N., & Rabin, M. (2021). Belief movement, uncertainty reduction, and rational updating. *Quarterly Journal of Economics*, 136(2), 933–985. https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjaa043 | Derived the excess-movement test of Bayesian updating and applied it to pooled GJP forecasts (593,218 assessments, 3,408 forecasters, 291 events): movement exceeded uncertainty reduction by 20%. | Splits excess movement by the time left until the question's scheduled close, restricted to forecasters who worked alone, so the result speaks to how updating changes with signal strength rather than to its average. Adds the training contrast and a reconstruction of their pooled statistic as a check. |
| 2 | Augenblick, N., Lazarus, E., & Thaler, M. (2025). Overinference from weak signals and underinference from strong signals. *Quarterly Journal of Economics*, 140(1), 335–401. https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjae032 | Showed over-inference from weak and under-inference from strong signals in experiments, and in Betfair and option prices, using time to resolution as the proxy for signal strength. Noted that the market results are "at minimum directionally informative" about individual beliefs. | Tests the prediction on individual, non-market probability reports in the field, with their own window regression. Separates the pattern from time-decay neglect (fixed-date versus deadline questions) and from a static compression of reports (calibration by horizon), using simulated predictions of each account on the same design. |
| 3 | Atanasov, P., Witkowski, J., Ungar, L., Mellers, B., & Tetlock, P. (2020). Small steps to accuracy: Incremental belief updaters are better forecasters. *Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes*, 160, 19–35. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.obhdp.2020.02.001 | In GJP, forecasters who updated often and in small steps were more accurate; training reduced update size by about 12%. | Judges updates against the Bayesian benchmark (movement relative to uncertainty reduction) instead of by size, and asks how this changes with horizon and whether training moves forecasters towards the benchmark or past it. |
| 4 | Moore, D. A., Swift, S. A., Minster, A., Mellers, B., Ungar, L., Tetlock, P., Yang, H. H. J., & Tenney, E. R. (2017). Confidence calibration in a multiyear geopolitical forecasting competition. *Management Science*, 63(11), 3552–3565. https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2016.2525 | Described GJP calibration over the life of a question: extreme forecasts made early were especially inaccurate, and confidence and accuracy rose together over time. | Links calibration by horizon to belief movement. The signal-strength account predicts overconfidence far from resolution and underconfidence near it; a static compression of reports predicts underconfidence throughout. This study tests both against frozen predictions. |
| 5 | Atanasov, P., & Himmelstein, M. (2023). Talent spotting in crowd prediction. In M. Seifert (Ed.), *Judgment in predictive analytics* (pp. 135–184). Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-30085-1_6 | Used the Augenblick–Rabin statistic per GJP forecaster as a stable skill marker (reliability .85; correlation with accuracy .30–.40). | Treats excess movement as a within-forecaster process that depends on horizon rather than as a trait, and estimates it separately for each horizon band. |

(2021, BIN model, accuracy components by horizon in GJP; https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2020.3882); Halperin and Mazlish (2025 working paper; the same sign pattern by horizon in consensus macroeconomic forecasts); Casey (2021; professional forecasters overconfident at long and underconfident at short horizons, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijforecast.2020.09.002).

# Novelty assessment before preregistration

Search completed 28 September 2026; primary sources, queries, metadata, and caveats are preserved in `scoping/literature_agent.md` and `scoping/journal_and_data.md`. This is a scoped search, not proof that no prior paper contains the same result. No hypothesis-bearing simulation or participant-level outcome was examined.

## Study contribution

The paper distinguishes two targets of learning from selectively verified advice: absolute advisor accuracy and the sign of the advisor's accuracy advantage over oneself. It derives the limits of paired comparison and quantifies finite-feedback decision loss when correction for confidence selection trades reduced bias for additional variance. A future randomised feedback-display experiment supplies refutable psychological predictions. The mathematical identity, inverse-probability weighting, and the general fact that selection biases learning are existing ideas, not claimed inventions.

## Five closest papers

1. **Pescetelli & Yeung (2021), The role of decision confidence in advice-taking and trust formation.** DOI: https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0000960. Their experiments and models concern confidence-weighted agreement as evidence of advisor reliability, including learning without objective feedback and distortion from dependent judgements. **Addition:** objective truth is available but selectively sampled; compare absolute and paired representations of the same verified cases and state their different estimands. This is not the first computational model of confidence and trust.

2. **Jaquiery & Yeung (2024), Preferences for advisor agreement and accuracy.** DOI: https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0311211. Their experiments distinguish agreement and accuracy with and without feedback; feedback supports preference for accuracy. **Addition:** distinguish feedback's presence from its selection mechanism; uniform disagreement feedback can remain adequate for relative ranking even when inappropriate for absolute assessment. No claim that their participants exhibited the proposed selection effect.

3. **Fetchenhauer & Dunning (2010), Why so cynical? Asymmetric feedback underlies misguided skepticism regarding the trustworthiness of others.** DOI: https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797609358586. Their trust experiments show that feedback conditional on trusting can sustain inaccurate negative impressions. **Addition:** advisor verification offers a paired contrast whose unobserved values on agreement are structurally zero, so missing feedback need not undermine the comparative decision. Reciprocity and classification accuracy are distinct tasks; this paper does not reproduce their experiment.

4. **Gao et al. (2021), Human-AI Collaboration with Bandit Feedback.** DOI: https://doi.org/10.24963/ijcai.2021/237. They use counterfactual policy learning to route cases between humans and machines under bandit feedback. **Addition:** a constrained global advisor-adoption decision, with fully verified paired labels on sampled cases, psychologically interpretable absolute/paired summaries, and finite-label cost of selection adjustment. IPW itself and learning from selectively observed outcomes are established; no general policy-learning advance is claimed.

5. **Zavattari, Tommasi, & Prencipe (2026), One Human, N Agents: Audit-Budget Allocation for LLM Agent Fleets under Miscalibrated, Correlated Confidence.** Primary preprint: https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28317. It already models budgeted inspections, confidence selection, correlated errors, and worse-than-random auditing. **Addition:** learning comparative competence from a feedback history rather than allocating inspections to reduce remaining errors across a fleet; paired representation and the zero contribution of agreements are central. This is an unreviewed preprint, and its DOI belongs to DataCite rather than Crossref; registry coverage must not be misrepresented.

## Further overlap and limits

Denrell & March (2001) and Denrell (2005) already explain biased impressions through selective experience. Fok & Weld (2024) discuss verification and complementary performance. Honeycutt et al. (2020) show that interactive feedback can reduce trust and perceived accuracy. Li & Steyvers (2026, preprint) model learning AI confidence calibration. These precedents restrict the contribution to a particular representation-by-selection boundary and its finite-feedback consequences.

A transparent two-stratum scenario is intentionally limited. The paper cannot establish which summaries humans use, how often real verification follows the assumed policies, or that its numerical worlds describe deployed AI. It should be judged as a computational Theory Article with a testable behavioural extension, not as empirical evidence of algorithm aversion.

## Post-preregistration literature addendum: selective-feedback coding

Added during the first manuscript review, after preregistration and confirmatory analysis, on 28 September 2026. This supplements the original five-paper assessment without changing the preregistration or the simulations.

**Elwin, Juslin, Olsson, and Enkvist (2007), Constructivist coding: Learning from selective feedback**, [10.1111/j.1467-9280.2007.01856.x](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9280.2007.01856.x), is a substantive predecessor. Their investment task contrasted complete with decision-contingent feedback. Performance was not demonstrably impaired by selective feedback, and behaviour was better captured by reconstructing missing outcomes from task knowledge than by merely recording observed outcomes. Their design also approximately matched feedback counts by allowing more training opportunities under selection. Primary full text and Crossref metadata were checked; see `manuscript/reference_audit.md`.

**Implication for contribution:** The general claims that selective experience need not damage decisions, that feedback representation matters, and that label-matched comparisons are useful are already established. This paper's narrower addition concerns absolute advisor accuracy versus the sign of a paired advisor–self accuracy difference, including the zero contribution of agreement cases and the finite-sample consequences of confidence-dependent selection within disagreements. Elwin et al. reconstruct unobserved outcomes for task learning and base-rate inference; the paired source-comparison identity and present estimator comparison are different. Their evidence is also a reason to treat the absolute learner as an experimental benchmark rather than an established default account of human learning.

import json, urllib.parse, urllib.request, os
def key():
    for l in open(os.path.expanduser("~/.claude/api_keys.env")):
        if l.startswith("OPENALEX_API_KEY_MANUAL="): return l.split("=",1)[1].strip().strip('"').strip("'")
def oa(path, params):
    params=dict(params); params["api_key"]=key()
    url="https://api.openalex.org/"+path+"?"+urllib.parse.urlencode(params)
    with urllib.request.urlopen(url,timeout=60) as r: return json.load(r)
def show(label, filt, n=8, sort="cited_by_count:desc"):

--- intertemporal dataset abstract ---
The study of intertemporal choices (ITC) plays a vital role in psychological and behavioral economics research. Models of intertemporal choice (ITC) have traditionally focused on choices. A growing interest in the underlying cognitive processes has initiated the development of process models. Process models require process data, and yet ITC research has largely overlooked even the simplest process data - response times (RTs). We present a large-scale dataset of choices and response times from 100 ITC studies with 11,852 subjects and 1,172,644 trials. In addition to behavioral data, we collected various methodological and sample information (e.g., task procedure, incentivization). The objective of the large-scale dataset is to facilitate the development of more nuanced and accurate theories of ITC. The associated ITC Database is open to ongoing submissions and is projected to expand continuously.

## 10.1037/xge0001414 | A unified explanation of variability and bias in human probability judgments: How computational noise explains the mean–variance signature.
    Human probability judgments are both variable and subject to systematic biases. Most probability judgment models treat variability and bias separately: a deterministic model explains the origin of bias, to which a noise process is added to generate variability. But these accounts do not explain the characteristic inverse U-shaped signature linking mean and variance in probability judgments. By contrast, models based on sampling generate the mean and variance of judgments in a unified way: the variability in the response is an inevitable consequence of basing probability judgments on a small sample of remembered or simulated instances of events. # Literature scouting report: candidate JDM research questions answerable without new data

Date: 28 September 2026
Scouter: opencode (literature scout)
Output of: scoping task for `ai-jdm-paper4`

---

## 0. Scope and constraints

This report proposes research questions in judgment and decision-making (JDM) that are (a) plausibly understudied, (b) answerable by **secondary analysis of openly licensed data** or by a **falsifiable simulation**, and (c) not covered by the three sibling papers:

- **Paper 1** (`ai-jdm-paper`) — anchoring/proportionality, OpAQ meta-analysis. **Excluded: anchoring.**
- **Paper 2** (`[other project]`) — GJP forecasting, belief movement by horizon. **Excluded: probability forecasting, GJP, belief-movement.**
- **Paper 3** (`ai-jdm-paper3`) — selective feedback / comparative advisor evaluation. **Excluded: advisor verification, selective feedback, advice-weight learning.**

The sibling `novelty.md` files were read in full before scouting. Where a candidate is close to a sibling paper's statistical machinery (e.g. excess-movement statistics, model-simulation-on-frozen-design), that is noted.

## 1. Method

- Sources searched: OpenAlex API (`title.search`, `title_and_abstract.search`, `cites:`), Crossref REST API (`query.bibliographic`), and journal-level sweeps of recent works (2023–2026) in *Judgment and Decision Making*, *Journal of Behavioral Decision Making*, *Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes*, *Cognitive Psychology*, *Cognition*, *Psychological Science*, and *Management Science* (source IDs: `S179575189`, `S117214846`, `S64744539`, `S36783443`, `S88198767`, `S58854535`, `S33323087`).
- Recent-issue sweeps and gap checks were run to detect (i) existing meta-analyses, (ii) existing large-scale/open-data reanalyses, and (iii) the closest conceptual neighbours for each candidate.
- Every DOI in this report was checked against Crossref (`https://api.crossref.org/works/{DOI}`). Two non-Crossref identifiers are flagged explicitly.

**Caveats (read these as limits on all novelty claims).**

- OpenAlex `title_and_abstract.search` requires all query terms and is therefore very restrictive; a low count is **not** evidence that a topic is absent from the literature. Conversely a high count is often noise. Counts below are indicative only.
- Google Scholar could not be queried. Unpublished working papers, dissertations, and very recent (in-press) articles may be missed. Several relevant items turned out to be preprints (flagged).
- "First meta-analysis" claims are stated conservatively: "no published quantitative synthesis was located in Crossref/OpenAlex searches dated 28 Sep 2026", not "none exists".

---

## 2. Candidates

### C1. The sunk-cost effect: first general quantitative synthesis

**Question.** How large is the sunk-cost / escalation-of-commitment effect across the human literature, and which moderators (decision domain, real vs. hypothetical stakes, action/inaction framing, individual differences in cognitive ability) explain the heterogeneity?

**Why novel / closest work and its gap.** The sunk-cost effect is a 40-year-old textbook bias with ~600 works whose title mentions it, yet no general meta-analysis was located. The only quantitative synthesis is confined to **IT-project escalation** (Keil, Li, Mathur, & Tan, 2007, *Information Resources Management Journal*, https://doi.org/10.4018/irmj.2007070101), and the closest broad treatment is a **narrative** cross-species review (Arkes & Ayton's tradition; Ferreira et al., 2016, *JEAB*, https://doi.org/10.1002/jeab.202). Two subsequent critical pieces (Arkes & Blumer's original is 1985) raise the possibility that the effect is an artifact of framing or of measurement (e.g. "Evaluating the Sunk Cost Effect", 2021, *JEBO*, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jebo.2021.03.029). Original anchor: Arkes & Blumer (1985), https://doi.org/10.1016/0749-5978(85)90049-4.

**Data / model needed.** Effect-size extraction from published studies (most are open-access or have OSF materials), plus any open raw datasets; where trial-level data are available, an individual-participant-data (IPD) two-stage meta-analysis with a multilevel model. A parallel **simulation** can show what design features (continuation vs. switching structure, scale of investment, whether "sunk" information is causally relevant) should moderate the effect, generating predictions that the meta-analysis then tests.

**Falsifiability.** Fully refutable. If the pooled effect is near zero after correcting for publication bias and selective reporting, or if moderators do not move it, the classic claim is weakened. The 2021 JEBO critique makes a null/small result a live possibility, which is exactly what makes the question worth answering.

**Feasibility risk.** Medium: requires manual effect-size coding rather than one clean open dataset. An IPD component depends on finding open raw data (many sunk-cost studies are now on OSF). This is the main candidate with a non-trivial extraction workload.

---

### C2. Overprecision (excessive precision in interval estimates): first quantitative synthesis

**Question.** How large is overprecision (confidence-interval hit rates below nominal coverage, and excessive narrowness), and how is it moderated by elicitation method (interval vs. distribution), incentives, item domain, and expertise?

**Why novel / closest work and gap.** Moore and Healy's (2008) *Psychological Review* paper, https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295x.115.2.502, is a conceptual reconciliation and reported that overprecision is the most persistent of the three overconfidence forms, but it is not a meta-analysis. The comprehensive treatment remains a **book chapter** (Moore, Tenney, & Haran, 2015, "Overprecision in Judgment", https://doi.org/10.1002/9781118468333.ch6). Crossref/OpenAlex searches located **no quantitative meta-analysis** of overprecision; the closest recent items are preprints (e.g. "Overprecision in Estimates of Physical Constants", 2025, https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/26b5s_v1; "Conversational Principles in Cognitive Biases: the Case of Overprecision in Interval Estimation", 2026, https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/rsuzd_v1). At the same time, overconfidence is being actively revived as an individual-difference construct (see §3), so the field is hot but unsynthesised on this face.

**Data / model needed.** Coverage rates and interval widths are extractable or computable from published studies; many recent studies release raw interval responses. A simulation is useful for the known **scale-usage confound** (hit rate depends on nominal level and item difficulty) — showing which "remedies" (e.g. the 2010 "simple remedy", https://doi.org/10.1017/s1930297500001637) actually move the target quantity vs. only re-scale reports.

**Falsifiability.** Refutable: the pooled overprecision effect could shrink substantially once the hard–easy/scale-usage confound is modelled, or could be heterogeneous to the point of uninterpretability.

**Feasibility risk.** Medium: same extraction concern as C1, mitigated by the large volume of open interval-response data.

---

### C3. Bias versus noise in human judgment across domains

**Question.** Across decision domains, what fraction of judgment error is systematic bias versus unsystematic noise, and does aggregation reduce noise faster than bias (i.e. can groups be accurate while individuals are noisy-but-biased in different directions)?

**Why novel / closest work and gap.** The bias–noise decomposition was popularised by Kahneman, Sibony, and Sunstein (2021, *Noise*), but it has rarely been operationalised across multiple domains with a common model. The closest academic paper, "A unified explanation of variability and bias in human probability judgments" (2023, *JEP: General*, https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0001414), models variability and bias jointly but **only for probability judgments**, and it addresses the mean–variance signature rather than a cross-domain bias/noise share or an aggregation comparison.

**Data / model needed.** Open datasets containing **repeated judgments of the same objects** by multiple judges (e.g. essay/translation quality grading, image/radiology ratings, perceptual estimation crowds; the Confidence Database, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-019-0813-1, supplies many repeated-trial tasks). A hierarchical variance-decomposition model (judge × item variance components) computes the bias and noise shares; a simulation then derives when aggregation helps more via noise cancellation vs. bias reduction.

**Falsifiability.** Refutable: if noise is small relative to bias in most domains, aggregation's role is limited; if bias dominates and is shared, crowds will not fix it. Either outcome is informative.

**Feasibility risk.** High: requires locating several open repeated-judgment datasets that share enough structure to pool; data access (not modelling) is the bottleneck. GJP forecasting data must **not** be used (paper 2).

---

### C4. When does confidence-weighting harm collective accuracy? Boundary conditions

**Question.** Under what joint distribution of confidence and error does weighting judges by their confidence **hurt** crowd accuracy relative to simple averaging, and where do real crowds sit relative to those boundaries?

**Why novel / closest work and gap.** Confidence-weighting is widely recommended (e.g. "Wisdom of crowds benefits perceptual decision making across difficulty levels", 2021, *Scientific Reports*, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-020-80500-0), and recent work models correlated estimates (Aczél-type "Bayesian combination of correlated subjective probability estimates", 2026, *JDM*, https://doi.org/10.1017/jdm.2026.10035). What appears missing is a **formal sufficiency/boundary analysis**: weight by confidence improves accuracy only under conditions on the confidence–error covariance and on shared bias; with miscalibration or shared error, confidence-weighting can amplify a common bias. A 2025 preprint, "The Weighting Bias" (https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.5205685), is adjacent and worth monitoring.

**Data / model needed.** Derive the condition analytically, then run an agent-based simulation sweeping confidence–accuracy coupling, shared bias, and within-crowd correlation. Validate on open crowd datasets that include confidence (Confidence Database; perceptual crowds). This is closer to paper 3's mode (simulation with frozen predictions) but targets aggregation, not advisor verification — the estimand and the decision problem differ.

**Falsifiability.** Mathematical claims are provable/falsifiable directly; empirical claims are refutable if real crowds never fall in the harmful region, or if re-weighting with the derived correction never helps.

**Feasibility risk.** Low-to-medium: simulation is fully controllable; validation datasets exist but confidence data are less standard than accuracy data.

---

### C5. Are "risk preference" and "patience" cross-nationally comparable? Measurement invariance in the Global Preferences Survey

**Question.** Are the Global Preferences Survey (GPS) risk and time-preference modules measurement-invariant across countries and language groups, and how much of the headline cross-country variation survives a proper invariance model?

**Why novel / closest work and gap.** The GPS (Falk et al., 2018, *QJE*, https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjy013; replication data https://doi.org/10.7910/dvn/hh8dv4) is one of the most reused open preference datasets, yet OpenAlex searches of its citers located **no measurement-invariance / comparability test** of its modules; the closest is a 2025 working paper, "Measuring Economic Preferences with Surveys and Behavioral Experiments" (https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.5114896). Cross-national preference comparisons assume comparability; this is exactly the assumption a large validation literature (psychometrics, cross-cultural methods) has shown often fails.

**Data / model needed.** GPS respondent-level data (open for research via the Bonn portal / Dataverse) and multi-group confirmatory factor / item-response models (configural, metric, scalar invariance) across countries; a simulation quantifies how much attenuation/country-ranking reshuffling non-invariance induces in commonly reported GPS summaries (e.g. country means, correlations with income).

**Falsifiability.** Refutable: if scalar invariance holds, the existing GPS comparisons are validated; if it fails, published rankings must be qualified. Under an "approximate invariance" framing, results are quantitative rather than binary, but still falsifiable against pre-set thresholds.

**Feasibility risk.** Low: one clean open dataset and standard models. Risk is that GPS authors or citers have an unpublished invariance appendix.

---

### C6. Do models of intertemporal choice generalise across 100 open studies — and do process models beat choice-only models?

**Question.** Which computational models of intertemporal choice best predict out-of-sample choices when estimated across the newly released multi-study database, and does adding response-time (process) information systematically improve prediction over choice-only models?

**Why novel / closest work and gap.** A 2026 *Scientific Data* paper released **"A large-scale dataset of choice and response-time data in intertemporal choice"**: 100 studies, 11,852 subjects, 1,172,644 trials, with study-level methodological metadata (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-026-06947-4; preprint https://doi.org/10.31219/osf.io/nezgk_v2). The dataset paper explicitly frames its purpose as enabling new theory development, and no work has yet used it for **cross-study generalisation** of models. Existing model comparisons are within-study (e.g. Nagel et al., 2025, https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-025-02709-2, compare attribute-wise vs. integrated models with a drift-diffusion framework in a single sample).

**Data / model needed.** The ITC database directly. Hierarchical Bayesian estimation of standard discounting models (exponential, hyperbolic, quasi-hyperbolic, attribute-wise) plus RT-enabled models (ddm/racing-diffusion), with study-level cross-validation and meta-regression on the provided metadata (incentivisation, procedure).

**Falsifiability.** Refutable: a single model might not generalise across studies (predicting failure of the "one best model" narrative), or process data might add nothing over choice data. Both are publishable outcomes.

**Feasibility risk.** Low-to-medium: the data are open and ready; the computational cost of hierarchical estimation over 1.17M trials is the main consideration. This is a strong, concrete candidate.

---

### C7. Is decision-strategy use domain-general or domain-specific?

**Question.** Do individuals who are best described by an "optimal" (expected-utility / Bayesian) strategy in risky choice also use optimal-style strategies in intertemporal choice, or is strategy use domain-specific and largely decoupled within person?

**Why novel / closest work and gap.** Model comparison in JDM is overwhelmingly **within-domain**. The closest cross-domain work compares ambiguity preferences and fits DDM across risk and time in a single large sample (Nagel et al., 2025, https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-025-02709-2), and the largest risky-choice modelling effort (Peterson et al., 2021, *Science*, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abe2629) is entirely within risky choice. No study appears to link individual-level strategy parameters **across** domains using large open datasets.

**Data / model needed.** CPC18 (Peterson et al., 2021; data/code released with the paper) for risky choice, and the ITC database (C6) for intertemporal choice. Estimate per-subject model parameters, then test cross-domain correlations and whether an "optimality" factor exists.

**Falsifiability.** Refutable and interesting either way: strong cross-domain correlations support a general decision-strategy factor; near-zero correlations support domain-specificity, challenging trait-like accounts of "decision competence".

**Feasibility risk.** Medium: CPC18 and the ITC database are separate samples (no within-person linkage), so the design is a between-sample comparison of parameter distributions unless a shared-sample open dataset is found. **Honest limitation:** some open datasets (e.g. Nagel et al., 2025) do contain both domains in one sample and should be checked for reuse rights first. Without within-person linkage this candidate is weaker; flag before committing.

---

### C8. Does the "inner crowd" gain depend on within-person error independence — or is it response noise?

**Question.** Does aggregating repeated judgments from a single person ("inner crowd") improve accuracy only when within-person errors are approximately independent, and how much of the reported gain is explained by response/scale noise rather than genuine "multiple perspectives"?

**Why novel / closest work and gap.** The inner crowd is claimed across several datasets (Herzog & Hertwig, 2017/2018, *Nature Human Behaviour*, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-017-0247-6; Herzog, von Helversen, & Hertwig, 2014, *TiCS*, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tics.2014.06.009; for confidence judgments, 2020, *Decision*, https://doi.org/10.1037/dec0000119). The proposed mechanism is that repeated within-person samples are collectively more accurate because errors partly cancel. What appears missing is a direct **noise-structure test**: is the benefit driven by genuine independent samples, or by averaging out response noise/rounding/scale usage? A simulation can define the expected gain under independence vs. correlated errors, and existing open repeated-judgment datasets can test which regime real data resemble.

**Data / model needed.** Open datasets with repeated judgments by the same individuals (a subset of the Confidence Database; large calibration datasets with repeated items). Model within-person error covariance; simulate the inner-crowd gain as a function of that covariance.

**Falsifiability.** Refutable: if within-person errors are strongly correlated, the inner crowd should give little gain, contradicting some reports; if gains persist, that supports genuine sampling.

**Feasibility risk.** Medium: depends on repeated-judgment datasets with identifiable subjects; some are available, but pooling across tasks is non-trivial.

---

## 3. Directions checked and set aside (crowded or out of scope)

Recorded so the same ground is not re-trodden:

- **Anchoring, probability forecasting/GJP, advisor verification/selective feedback** — excluded by the brief (sibling papers).
- **Confidence Database reanalysis for domain-generality of metacognition** — crowded. The database (Rahnev et al., 2020, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-019-0813-1) already has a direct *meta-analysis of confidence–accuracy* (https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-022-02063-7), plus domain-generality papers (https://doi.org/10.1177/17456916221075615; https://doi.org/10.1038/s44159-023-00245-1; https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0001197). Do not propose a generic Confidence Database question.
- **Overconfidence as an individual difference** — actively worked: *JDM* 2025 https://doi.org/10.1017/jdm.2025.11; *Cognition* 2026 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2026.106665. (C2 targets overprecision *magnitude/moderation*, which is distinct, but cross-reference these.)
- **Choice overload, description–experience gap, identifiable victim effect, omission bias, status-quo bias (IS adoption), nudge/default effects** — meta-analyses already exist (choice overload: https://doi.org/10.1086/651235; description–experience: https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000115; identifiable victim: https://doi.org/10.1080/15534510.2016.1216891; omission bias: https://doi.org/10.1177/01461672211042315; defaults: https://doi.org/10.1017/bpp.2018.43).
- **Serial dependence in perception** — heavily reviewed (https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-psych-021523-104939), and a 2026 *Cognition* paper already covers serial effects in choice and confidence (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2026.106643).
- **Hot-hand / gambler's-fallacy belief–reality correspondence** — attractive and plausibly under-tested as a **cross-domain** correspondence question (anchors: Gilovich et al., 1985, https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-0285(85)90010-6; Miller & Sanjurjo, 2018, https://doi.org/10.3982/ecta14943; MLB equilibrium, https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2017.2804). Not promoted to a main candidate because it likely needs *belief* data across domains that may not exist openly (risk of requiring new data), but it is the strongest fallback if C7's within-person linkage cannot be secured.

---

## 4. Ranking summary

| # | Candidate | Open data / simulation | Novelty signal | Feasibility |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| C1 | Sunk-cost first general meta-analysis | Effect sizes + open raw (IPD) | High (no general meta located) | Medium (extraction) |
| C6 | ITC model generalisation across 100 studies | Open 1.17M-trial database | High (new dataset, unused) | Low–medium |
| C5 | GPS measurement invariance | Single clean open dataset | High (untested comparability) | Low |
| C4 | Confidence-weighting harm boundaries | Simulation + open crowd data | High (formal gap) | Low–medium |
| C2 | Overprecision first meta-analysis | Effect sizes + open raw | High (no meta located) | Medium |
| C8 | Inner-crowd noise-structure test | Open repeated-judgment data + simulation | Medium–high | Medium |
| C3 | Bias vs. noise across domains | Open repeated-judgment data | Medium–high | High (data access) |
| C7 | Cross-domain strategy consistency | CPC18 + ITC database | Medium (adjacent work exists) | Medium (no within-person link) |

## 5. Recommendation

The strongest combination of novelty and feasibility is **C1**, **C6**, **C5**, and **C4**: one clear "first-ever synthesis" (sunk cost), one large ready-made open dataset with a clean gap (intertemporal choice), one measurement-validity reanalysis (GPS), and one formal simulation with an empirical test (confidence-weighting). **C3** is the most scientifically interesting but the most data-constrained; **C7** must resolve the within-person linkage question before commitment.
